journey.lifecycle.prepare.summary.message: A node both wallets can reach, and a sender holding spendable outputs. Whether the receiver has to be online depends on the transport.

journey.lifecycle.draft.summary.message: The sender builds a partial slate and reserves the selected outputs locally. Nothing is on the chain yet, and only a cancellation releases the reservation.

journey.lifecycle.deliver.summary.message: The slate reaches the receiver as a file you move, an HTTP request, or a message queued by a relay. This is the step that fails in practice.

journey.lifecycle.cosign.summary.message: The receiver adds an output, its range proof and a partial signature, then returns the slate the same way it arrived.

journey.lifecycle.post.summary.message: The sender completes the aggregate signature and posts the transaction. If the exchange cannot finish, cancel it deliberately to release the reserved outputs.

slateExchange.completes.step1.message: The sender asks the node for the chain tip, builds a slate, and reserves the inputs it will spend.

slateExchange.completes.step2.message: The sender posts the slate straight to the receiver’s listener.

slateExchange.completes.step3.message: The receiver adds their half and signs.

slateExchange.completes.step4.message: The signed slate comes back in the same response.

slateExchange.completes.step5.message: The sender finalises it and posts it to the node, which broadcasts it.

slateExchange.receiverAway.step1.message: The sender builds a slate and reserves the inputs it will spend.

slateExchange.receiverAway.step2.message: Nothing is listening on the receiver’s address, so the request fails.

slateExchange.receiverAway.step3.message: One half is signed, so there is nothing to finalise.

slateExchange.receiverAway.step4.message: The reserved inputs stay reserved. Cancelling the transaction returns them.

slateExchange.senderAway.step1.message: The sender builds a slate and reserves the inputs it will spend.

slateExchange.senderAway.step2.message: The sender posts the slate straight to the receiver’s listener.

slateExchange.senderAway.step3.message: The receiver adds their half and signs.

slateExchange.senderAway.step4.message: The sender is gone, so the signed slate has nowhere to return to. Nothing holds it for later.

slateExchange.senderAway.step5.message: Nothing finalises, and the reserved inputs stay reserved until the transaction is cancelled.

slateExchange.noNode.step1.message: A wallet reads the chain and posts through a node, so the send contacts one first.

slateExchange.noNode.step2.message: With none reachable the send stops before a slate exists, so no inputs are reserved.

slateExchange.noNode.step3.message: Point the wallet at a node it can reach, then send again.

slateExchange.epicbox.step1.message: The sender encrypts the slate and posts it to the relay.

slateExchange.epicbox.step2.message: The relay holds it until the receiver’s wallet connects. The two wallets never have to be online at the same time.

slateExchange.epicbox.step3.message: The receiver collects it, adds their half and signs.

slateExchange.epicbox.step4.message: The signed slate goes back to the relay, which holds it until the sender returns.

slateExchange.epicbox.step5.message: The sender comes back online and collects the signed slate from the relay.

slateExchange.epicbox.step6.message: The sender finalises it and posts it to the node, which broadcasts it.

slateExchange.epicbox.step7.message: Confirmations bury the output, and the receiver can spend it.

diagram.slateRounds.step1.title.message: The sender builds a partial slate

diagram.slateRounds.step1.body.message: init_send_tx selects inputs and writes the first round. tx_lock_outputs then reserves those inputs locally, before the receiver has done anything.
diagram.slateRounds.step1.body.description: Slate exchange diagram, step 1 detail. Keep init_send_tx and tx_lock_outputs as written.

diagram.slateRounds.step2.title.message: The slate travels to the receiver

diagram.slateRounds.step2.body.message: A file you move, an HTTP request, or a message queued by a relay. The transport is the part that fails in practice.

diagram.slateRounds.step3.body.message: receive_tx adds an output, its range proof and a partial signature, so the slate now carries two participants.
diagram.slateRounds.step3.body.description: Slate exchange diagram, step 3 detail. Keep receive_tx as written.

diagram.slateRounds.step4.title.message: The slate comes back the same way

diagram.slateRounds.step4.body.message: Over epicbox this arrives asynchronously, which is why the sender also needs a listener running.

diagram.slateRounds.step5.body.message: finalize_tx completes the aggregate signature and post_tx broadcasts it. Only now does a node see a transaction at all.
diagram.slateRounds.step5.body.description: Slate exchange diagram, step 5 detail. Keep finalize_tx and post_tx as written.

diagram.slateRounds.caption.message: One transfer, two rounds. Nothing reaches the chain until step 05.
diagram.slateRounds.caption.description: Caption under the slate exchange diagram

diagram.slateRounds.receiverWallet.description: Slate diagram, label on the receiving party box

diagram.slateRounds.addsOutput.description: Slate diagram, what the receiver does. Keep it short.

diagram.slateRounds.signsOnce.description: Slate diagram, what the receiver does. Two words if possible.

diagram.slateRounds.roundOne.description: Slate diagram, label on the first transport arrow

diagram.slateRounds.roundTwo.description: Slate diagram, label on the return transport arrow

diagram.slateRounds.transports.description: Slate diagram, the three transports. These are transport names; keep them as written.

diagram.slateRounds.node.description: Slate diagram, label on the node box. One word.

diagram.slateRounds.mempoolThenBlock.description: Slate diagram, what happens after posting. Keep mempool as written.

diagram.handshake.step1.title.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 1 heading

diagram.handshake.step1.body.message: A secp256k1 keypair in your client, used once per session.
diagram.handshake.step1.body.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 1 detail. Keep secp256k1 as written.

diagram.handshake.step2.body.message: Send your compressed public key. The wallet replies with its own. This is the only unencrypted call.
diagram.handshake.step2.body.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 2 detail

diagram.handshake.step3.title.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 3 heading

diagram.handshake.step3.body.message: Multiply the wallet key by your scalar and keep the raw x coordinate, 32 bytes, unhashed. Hashing it is the most common implementation mistake.
diagram.handshake.step3.body.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 3 detail

diagram.handshake.step4.title.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 4 heading. open_wallet is a method name; keep it.

diagram.handshake.step4.body.message: The first call inside encrypted_request_v3. It needs the wallet password and returns a token.
diagram.handshake.step4.body.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 4 detail. Keep encrypted_request_v3 as written.

diagram.handshake.step5.title.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 5 heading

diagram.handshake.step5.body.message: AES-256-GCM with a fresh 12-byte nonce, the 16-byte tag appended to the ciphertext, and the token in the params.
diagram.handshake.step5.body.description: Owner API handshake diagram, step 5 detail. Keep AES-256-GCM and params as written.

diagram.handshake.caption.message: The handshake, once per session. Everything after step 03 is encrypted.
diagram.handshake.caption.description: Caption under the Owner API handshake diagram

diagram.handshake.yourClient.description: Handshake diagram, label on the caller lane

diagram.handshake.walletPublicKey.description: Handshake diagram, what the wallet sends back

diagram.handshake.encryptedRequest.description: Handshake diagram, the first encrypted call. Both names are identifiers; keep them.

diagram.handshake.tokenEncrypted.description: Handshake diagram, what comes back from open_wallet. Two or three words.
